prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock and its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18, opening new precision tests of nature

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a discovery in the sense I care about most: a clue pulled out of nature by measurement. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removed the trade-off between many atoms and perturbation-free interrogation, and Ye's group took the clock to the 10^-18 regime, including resolving the gravitational redshift across millimetres and many-body effects in the clock. The payoff is physics and not only metrology: tests of relativity and of the constancy of constants, searches for dark-matter signatures, and relativistic geodesy. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, with two names that match the two decisive steps. Six of eight members ranked it, four of them first, and the reasons given are independent of each other (precision, reproducibility across JILA, Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, and a clear separation from the comb and ion-control prizes). After hearing everyone I still see no other entry that combines an unambiguous discovery, a clean credit list and full maturity.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is lineage. Time and frequency has already been honoured in 2005 (the frequency comb) and 2012 (control of single ions), and a sceptic can call the lattice clock an incremental refinement of a recognised programme, with the real societal endorsement (a redefinition of the second) still pending. There is also a risk that a prize for an instrument is read as engineering. Credit is also not perfectly tidy: Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups contributed to the ecosystem, and I am working from recollection and the supplied list rather than from primary priority documents.

responses.point: Eva Olsson ranks the tunnel magnetoresistance entry (B038) first as an original, verified experiment with large technological use, and ranks the lattice clock third, noting the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree on the overlap question and take it seriously, but I think it counts against B038 more than against B022. The 2007 GMR prize sits directly beside TMR, and by her own account the MgO giant-TMR priority belongs partly to Yuasa and colleagues who are outside the credited names, so the trio is not a faithful description of the discovery. The lattice clock rests on a different physical idea (magic-wavelength trapping) from the comb or ion control. I would still want her to say whether the 1995 Miyazaki-Moodera result is sufficiently distinct from GMR as a discovery rather than a device improvement, because I could be moved if the committee judged B038 to be a separate phenomenon.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson puts dynamical mean-field theory (B018) first, as a controllable, non-perturbative framework tied to real materials, and ranks magic-angle graphene (B028) second.
responses.response: I respect the weight of DMFT, but my reservation is the one Bernhard Mehlig himself raises: it is an approximation scheme, exact only in infinite dimensions, and the case for it as a discovery of nature rather than a method is thin, quite apart from Metzner being absent from the credit list. That is why I keep it off my configuration. I do share his enthusiasm for the moire candidate B028, which is a surprise delivered by a geometric knob, and I agree it is the most natural alternative if the committee wants condensed matter. I remain wary of the unsettled pairing mechanism, which he also flags.

responses.point: Mark Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino entry (B002) first as the opening of a new observational window, with Halzen as the single credited name, and ranks the lattice clock second.
responses.response: I put B002 fifth and I think the disagreement is mostly about attribution and maturity rather than the merit of neutrino astronomy. The diffuse flux is solid, but the individual source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are still at a modest significance, and a one-person prize for a large collaboration and its AMANDA predecessor invites exactly the credit dispute Mark himself acknowledges. If the committee could settle on a broader, defensible set of names I would move B002 up, but the shortlist as supplied does not allow it. His second-place ranking of the clock suggests that B022 could be a robust consensus choice.

responses.point: Stefan Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a step change in measurement precision, and puts atom interferometry (B004) second on the same principle that progress is limited by measurement.
responses.response: We agree on B022, but I qualify the reasoning for B004. Four credited names for three places already means a real person is left out (Schmiedmayer), and Steven Chu, an obvious contributor named by Eva Lindroth, is not on the list at all. The fundamental-physics reach, in terms of equivalence-principle tests and gravitational-wave detection, is still prospective, so the case rests on instruments more than on a result from nature. I would keep it out of my alternatives for that reason, although I understand why an experimentalist values it.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first and the optical-lattice quantum simulation entry (B020) second, but warns that the allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Cirac and Esslinger is genuinely contested and that Zoller and Cirac also appear in other candidates.
responses.response: I agree with her first choice. On B020 I share her unease and would go further: my own opening put it sixth because its impact on discoveries in nature is still mostly about methods, and choosing three from five is partly arbitrary. I keep it as an alternative only because it has the broadest support after the clock (Johansson and Lindroth rank it second) and the field is mature. If it came to a joint configuration, the clock plus a quantum-simulation part would exceed three people, so I do not propose combining them.

responses.point: Bernhard Mehlig ranks two-dimensional melting and the hexatic phase (B011) first, as a foundational, overdue statistical-physics mechanism, while acknowledging that it overlaps conceptually with the 2016 prize and that experimental melting scenarios vary between systems.
responses.response: This is a serious case on merit and I do not dismiss it: the theory is textbook and the credit trio is clean. My difficulty is the one he names himself. After Kosterlitz and Thouless in 2016 the novelty has to be argued as the hexatic step, and the fact that some real systems melt first-order weakens the claim that nature has confirmed one scenario. It also had only two members ranking it. I would be glad to hear whether he sees the experimental colloidal evidence as decisive, because that is the argument that could make it more than an overdue theory prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or would prefer to wait for the redefinition of the second.
Whether the credit should reach beyond Katori and Ye to other lattice-clock pioneers such as Lemonde or Gill; I have not verified priority from primary sources.
Which condensed-matter or quantum-simulation entry, B028 or B020, would be the stronger fallback if the clock fails to gather a majority.
Whether MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero alone, without Bistritzer, would be an acceptable moire configuration if B028 became the preferred candidate.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My connections (David Gross as PhD supervisor, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string-theory group) are in theory of gravity and cosmology and none of the credited names on the shortlist are linked to them.
